method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar index is holding near a three-week low around 101.7 because markets expect the Fed to wait until December to raise rates; it meets on October 27–28. Costly oil keeps that hike in view, which stops the dollar from falling much further.

EUR.text: France's 10-year borrowing cost passed 5% for the first time since 2002 and its gap over Germany is the widest since the euro debt crisis, as the budget fight and violent protests drag on. That keeps the euro below $1.125 and near a three-month low on the franc, with France's budget vote on October 27.

GBP.text: UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September, above forecast, which all but locks in a Bank of England rate hike on November 5. Government borrowing also came in above forecast before the October 28 budget, so debt worries kept the pound near 1.34 rather than higher.

JPY.text: Bank of Japan Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino said inflation is near target, backing a hike most expect in December, which helps the yen over time. For now, oil near $110 and a wider trade deficit keep it weak near 158 per dollar.

CHF.text: Stalled US-Iran peace efforts, drone alarms over Saudi Arabia and France's debt worries all keep demand for the franc high, near a three-month high on the euro. The Swiss National Bank has warned it may act to stop it rising too far.

CAD.text: The loonie is near a one-month high as traders now see a Bank of Canada rate hike on October 28 as likely and oil sits near $110. Some strategists argue markets expect too many hikes, since core inflation is below the bank's 2% target.

AUD.text: The Aussie reached a one-month high above 70 US cents as Reserve Bank of Australia officials warned inflation may run hotter, keeping a November 3 hike possible. Faster-than-expected growth in China, its biggest customer, adds support.

NZD.text: Markets give about 80% odds that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand hikes on October 28. The kiwi paused before the quarterly inflation figure, due within a day and expected at 3.8%, which will firm up or shake that bet.

XAU.text: Gold bounced to about $4,133 on Wednesday as oil eased, but it has been stuck between $4,100 and $4,200 for 16 days. Markets see a Fed rate hike in December as very likely, which keeps a lid on it.

OIL.text: Oil is still near five-month highs, held up by worsening Iranian attacks on ships near Hormuz and stalled US-Iran peace talks. It slipped back on Wednesday afternoon, with US crude near $96, after the US let some sanctioned cargo be delivered and Russia agreed in principle to new Ukraine peace talks.

items.headline: Gold rebounds above $4,130 as Oil retreats, Fed decision looms
items.story_title: Gold: oil, yields and the Fed
items.summary: Gold bounced back to about $4,133 after three days of losses, as oil slipped and the dollar eased, but it's still stuck in the same narrow range.

beats.was: Gold is down about a quarter from its record near $5,600 because costly oil has pushed the US Federal Reserve toward raising interest rates, which makes gold, paying no interest, less attractive. It has traded between $4,100 and $4,200 for 16 days in a row.
beats.happened: Gold rose to about $4,133 after touching $4,106 earlier on Wednesday, helped by a dip in oil after a US sanctions licence and a slightly weaker dollar. Markets still see about an 89% chance the Fed raises rates in December, and a small chance at its October 27–28 meeting.
beats.means: The bounce is small and doesn't change the bigger picture: as long as a Fed rate hike is expected, gold struggles to climb. Cheaper oil would ease that pressure.
beats.fx: Oil dips → slightly less pressure for Fed hikes → gold lifts a little. The lens: still inside its range; the Fed meeting next week matters more.

impact.why: A small rebound as oil and the dollar eased.
The dollar slipped slightly as oil fell.

items.watch: The Fed's October 27–28 decision and next week's US core inflation (PCE) figure.

items.headline: Risk-on trade as desks cite OFAC authorising offloading of some cargo involving some blocked vessels
items.story_title: US sanctions on Iran's oil shipping
items.summary: The US Treasury let some cargo be unloaded from tankers it had just blacklisted, and oil slipped while shares, bonds and gold rose.

beats.was: The US is at war with Iran and blocks Iranian oil exports, adding tankers and shipping firms to its sanctions list most weeks. Oil had climbed back near five-month highs on Wednesday morning as peace talks stalled.
beats.happened: The US Treasury's sanctions office (OFAC) blacklisted nine more vessels and several shipping firms on Wednesday, but issued a licence allowing some of their cargo to be unloaded and their business wound down. US crude fell about 80 cents soon after, and the dollar eased.
beats.means: Oil already at sea may still reach buyers instead of being stuck, so a little less supply goes missing. The licence is narrow, and past ones like it have had little lasting effect.
beats.fx: Some blocked oil can still be delivered → slightly more supply → small dip in oil prices → mild relief for oil importers like Japan and Europe, a small drag on the Canadian dollar. The lens: a narrow, technical step, not a change in US policy.

impact.why: Lets some sanctioned cargo reach buyers, easing supply worries a little.
Gold rose as bond yields and the dollar eased on the move.
The dollar slipped as cheaper oil eased Fed rate-hike worries.

items.watch: Whether the US widens the licence, or new sanctions follow that block more Iranian oil.

items.headline: US crude stocks fall 3.06 million barrels, more than the 0.82 million expected
items.story_title: US oil stocks: a run of draws
items.summary: Official US figures showed crude and gasoline stocks both fell more than expected last week, the second big weekly drop in a row.

beats.was: Oil has been near five-month highs because attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea threaten Gulf supply. The week before, US crude stocks fell about 8.6 million barrels, and an industry estimate on Tuesday had pointed to another large drop.
beats.happened: The US Energy Information Administration said crude stocks fell about 3.1 million barrels in the week to October 16, against about 0.8 million expected. Gasoline stocks fell about 3 million barrels, while diesel and heating oil stocks rose.
beats.means: America is drawing down its own stored oil while Gulf supply is at risk, so there is less cushion if shipping gets worse. The drop was smaller than Tuesday's industry estimate, so US crude barely moved, near $98.
beats.fx: Shrinking US oil stocks → less spare supply → keeps oil prices firm → helps the Canadian dollar, weighs on big oil importers like Japan. The lens: mostly expected after Tuesday's estimate, so the push is small.

impact.why: A second large weekly fall in US stocks adds to supply worries, though much was already expected.
Firm oil prices support Canada's export income.

items.watch: Next week's US stock figures and any news on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

items.headline: Yemen's Houthis deny launching drones towards Saudi Arabia's Medina
items.story_title: Houthis widen attacks on Saudi Arabia
items.summary: Saudi-led forces said they shot down drones over Medina and the oil-rich Eastern region; Yemen's Houthi movement denied sending them, leaving it unclear who is behind the attack.

beats.was: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group restarted fighting with Saudi Arabia this month, ending a 2022 truce. It has hit Riyadh's airport and Saudi Aramco oil sites, opening another front in the US-Israeli war with Iran.
beats.happened: The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted drones over the holy city of Medina and the Eastern region, where most Saudi oil is produced. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched none and is not attacking Saudi Arabia. Inside Yemen, the Houthis claimed an attack near Aden's airport.
beats.means: Drones are still reaching Saudi oil country, but the mixed claims make it hard to tell whether the Saudi front is widening or not.
beats.fx: Drones over Saudi oil regions → risk to the world's largest oil exporter → keeps a war premium in oil. The lens: confirmed damage to Saudi oil sites would push it higher; a clear Houthi pull-back would ease it.

impact.why: Drones over Saudi oil country keep supply worries alive, though no damage is reported.
Another sign of a wider Gulf conflict keeps some demand for safe havens.

items.watch: Any confirmed hit on Saudi oil sites or exports, and whether the Houthis' denial holds.

items.headline: USA to Tap National Diesel Reserve
items.story_title: US fuel prices before the midterms
items.summary: The US government will lend out a third of its emergency heating-oil stock in the Northeast to cool diesel prices before the November 3 elections.

beats.was: The war with Iran has pushed US diesel to record highs; it averages about $6.32 a gallon, and the midterm elections are on November 3. The Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve holds 1 million barrels for winter emergencies.
beats.happened: US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the government will lend 315,000 barrels from that reserve, with deliveries done by November 13. He called it a temporary fix for a temporary supply problem.
beats.means: The amount is tiny next to what the US uses each day, so the effect on prices is mostly symbolic. It shows Washington is under pressure to bring fuel costs down quickly.
beats.fx: Small emergency fuel release → barely more supply → little change to oil prices. The lens: a political signal more than a market one.

impact.why: Adds a small amount of diesel supply and signals Washington wants lower fuel prices.

items.watch: Whether the government releases more from its emergency stocks if prices keep rising.

items.headline: Iran Intensifies Strikes on Ships
items.story_title: Hormuz: reopening offer vs ship attacks
items.summary: Attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz are getting more frequent and more damaging, with missiles replacing drones and two vessels sunk last week.

beats.was: About a fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the US-Iran war began. Iran has been attacking ships there to pressure Washington while peace talks run through Pakistan and Qatar.
beats.happened: At least 23 attacks on ships were logged in or near the strait in the first two weeks of October, at least five of them hitting engine rooms, which hadn't happened in September. Iran is using more missiles, and at least two ships sank last week.
beats.means: Oil is still flowing: Gulf exports are close to pre-war levels by some counts. But each attack makes tankers scarcer and shipping and insurance dearer, which keeps a risk premium in oil.
beats.fx: Heavier ship attacks → costlier, riskier Gulf shipping → keeps oil prices firm → helps the Canadian dollar, weighs on importers like Japan, and supports safe havens like the Swiss franc. The lens: escalation in kind, but flows are holding up.

impact.why: Worse ship attacks raise shipping costs and the risk of lost supply.
More violence at sea keeps demand for safe havens.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so costlier shipping hurts its trade balance.

items.watch: Any sign that Gulf oil exports fall back below normal, or that attacks ease if talks make progress.

items.headline: Putin ready to resume three-way Ukraine peace talks
items.story_title: Russia–Ukraine: peace talks restart?
items.summary: After meeting the US envoy, Russia's President Vladimir Putin agreed in principle to new peace talks with the US and Ukraine, possibly in Abu Dhabi in mid-November.

beats.was: US-brokered talks to end the Russia-Ukraine war stalled in February, before the US-Iran war began. The war keeps European energy costly and adds to worries about Russian sabotage in NATO countries.
beats.happened: US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin for three hours in St Petersburg on Wednesday, a day after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo. Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said Russia is willing in principle to hold three-way talks, maybe in Abu Dhabi in mid-November, though he called Europe's and Kyiv's latest ideas thin.
beats.means: A restart of talks is a step, not a deal: the two sides remain far apart on terms. Still, it slightly lowers the odds of a wider war on Europe's edge.
beats.fx: Peace talks may resume → a little less war risk for Europe → mild support for the euro, and a small drag on oil if Russian supply looks safer. The lens: early, and talks have failed before.

impact.why: Any easing of the war next door lifts Europe's outlook a little.
Peace hopes trim the risk to Russian energy supply.

items.watch: Whether a date and place for the talks is confirmed, and whether Ukraine and Europe agree to join.

items.headline: US sends more warships as Iran peace push stalls over enriched uranium
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: Iran's top security official told Pakistan's army chief that none of Iran's enriched uranium will leave the country, while the US sent another carrier group and some 9,000 sailors and Marines to the region.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since earlier this year and the Strait of Hormuz, the main Gulf oil route, is shut. Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, has been carrying a plan to restart talks.
beats.happened: Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said no enriched uranium will be sent abroad, a key US demand. President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran won't talk under threat. The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier group and an amphibious group are heading in, and President Trump is said to be weighing new strikes. Gulf stock markets fell.
beats.means: The two sides are stuck on the same nuclear point, and the US is adding force rather than easing off, so a quick reopening of Hormuz looks less likely.
beats.fx: Stalled talks + more warships → Hormuz stays shut longer → oil supply stays tight → firmer oil, steadier demand for safe havens like the franc. The lens: any sign Iran would ship uranium out would reverse this.

impact.why: A stalled peace push and a bigger US fleet point to the oil route staying closed.
Rising war risk keeps money looking for safety.
Canada exports oil, so dearer crude helps its trade income.

items.watch: Whether Trump orders new strikes, and any change in Iran's line on shipping uranium abroad.

items.headline: Rubio calls an Iran peace deal 'extremely difficult' as pressure stays on
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a peace deal with Iran will be very hard to reach and that economic pressure stays until Iran stops hitting ships near Hormuz.

beats.was: Hopes for a US-Iran deal briefly pulled oil lower on Monday and Tuesday, after reports of a plan to restart talks.
beats.happened: Rubio said economic pressure will continue until Tehran stops targeting commercial shipping. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran wants a peaceful end but sees no US will to agree and is ready to defend itself.
beats.means: Both governments are now publicly playing down a deal, which takes away the reason oil dipped earlier this week.
beats.fx: Lower deal hopes → shipping risk stays → oil holds up → helps oil exporters' currencies, weighs on big oil importers like Japan. The lens: talk of a date for direct talks would change the picture.

impact.why: Fading deal hopes remove the reason oil fell earlier in the week.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so dearer crude widens its import bill.

items.watch: Any date or venue for direct US-Iran talks; further attacks on ships near Hormuz.

items.headline: Gold falls for a fourth session as oil revives rate-hike bets
items.story_title: Gold: oil, yields and the Fed
items.summary: Gold slipped to around $4,117–4,120 an ounce, a fourth straight daily fall, as higher oil revived bets that the Federal Reserve raises rates in December.

beats.was: Gold climbed to records through the year, but the Gulf war's oil shock has pushed up inflation and with it the chance of higher US interest rates, which hurt a metal that pays no interest.
beats.happened: Oil rose after a diplomat played down talk of an imminent US-Iran deal, and gold edged down about 0.1–0.2%. The Fed is expected to hold next week, with a December hike seen as possible.
beats.means: For now gold is trading more on US rate expectations than as a war shelter.
beats.fx: Costlier oil → higher US inflation → more chance of a Fed hike → less appeal for gold. The lens: a real fall in US yields would turn this.

impact.why: Rate-hike bets keep weighing on a metal that pays no interest.

items.watch: Next week's Fed meeting and any shift in December hike odds; a lasting drop in oil.

items.headline: Middle East War: Iran rejects US terms as tanker explodes near Hormuz
items.story_title: US-Iran: talks on reopening Hormuz
items.summary: Iran turned down US-backed Pakistani talks proposals and said its enriched uranium will not leave the country, while the US is reported to be sending a third aircraft carrier to the region.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, has been shut for months by the US-Iran war, and Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir is in Tehran trying to restart talks.
beats.happened: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said there are no talks until the US meets seven Iranian conditions. Parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Iran had nothing new to say. Fox News reported a third US carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is heading to the region.
beats.means: Tuesday's hopes for a deal have faded, and both sides are hardening. A reopening of the strait looks further away.
beats.fx: Less hope of a deal → oil stays high → support for oil-exporter Canada's dollar, pressure on oil-importer Japan's yen, and demand for shelter like the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Iran's refusal pushes a reopening of Hormuz further off.
More conflict risk adds demand for a safe place to park money.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a higher oil bill weighs on the yen.
Higher oil helps Canada, a big oil exporter.

items.watch: Any US decision on new strikes, or a fresh offer from Pakistan or Qatar that Iran accepts.

items.headline: Oil rises as Iran tensions, US crude stock draw fuel supply concerns
items.story_title: Hormuz: reopening offer vs ship attacks
items.summary: Brent crude climbed back to about $110 a barrel after Iran's leaders cooled talk of a deal and an industry estimate showed US crude stocks fell more than expected.

beats.was: Brent had dropped to about $106 on Tuesday on reports of a Qatar-Pakistan compromise plan between the US and Iran.
beats.happened: It rose about 1.5% to near $110.5 after Iran said it would not trust Washington without its conditions being met. The American Petroleum Institute estimated US crude stocks fell about 4.9 million barrels last week, versus about 1.3 million expected.
beats.means: Tuesday's fall was a reaction to hope, not supply. With no deal and US stocks shrinking, the oil price is back where it was.
beats.fx: Oil near $110 → more inflation pressure in oil importers → weighs on the yen and euro, helps the Canadian dollar. Official US stock figures from the Energy Information Administration come later Wednesday.

impact.why: A bigger-than-expected US stock fall adds to supply worries.
Higher oil supports Canada's export income.
A costlier oil bill weighs on Japan.

items.watch: The official US Energy Information Administration stock figures, due 9:30 AM CT Wednesday.

items.headline: France's 10-year bond yield climbs above 5%, stirring fears of a credit crisis
items.story_title: France: budget fight, protests and debt worries
items.summary: France now pays over 5% to borrow for ten years, the first time since 2002, and the gap over German debt is the widest since the euro debt crisis of 2009–2011.

beats.was: France's government has no majority to pass spending cuts, its debt is about 119% of the economy, and student protests have turned violent, with partial curfews in some cities. The budget vote is due October 27.
beats.happened: The 10-year French government bond yield went above 5%. The extra yield over Germany's 10-year bond widened to roughly 1.6 percentage points, a level last seen in the 2009–2011 crisis.
beats.means: Investors are asking more to lend to France because they doubt it can control its debt before next year's election. That worry spills into the euro as a whole.
beats.fx: French borrowing costs up + wider gap to Germany → doubts about the euro area's weakest big borrower → money leaves the euro for safer homes like the franc. The lens: a budget deal or calmer protests would ease it.

impact.why: Higher French borrowing costs feed doubts about the euro area and cap the euro's recovery.
Stress inside the euro area sends money to the Swiss franc next door.

items.watch: The October 27 budget vote, this weekend's protests, and Moody's review of France's credit rating on Friday.

items.headline: Australian Dollar extends recovery as hawkish RBA offsets USD strength
items.story_title: RBA: the November 3 decision
items.summary: The Australian dollar reached a one-month high near 70.3 US cents, a fourth day of gains, as Reserve Bank of Australia officials kept the door open to a November hike.

beats.was: The Aussie fell below 69 US cents last week, its lowest since early July, before Reserve Bank of Australia officials turned more worried about inflation.
beats.happened: Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser warned that underlying inflation for July-September may come in hotter than forecast, and Assistant Governor Christopher Kent said the 'neutral' rate, neither boosting nor slowing the economy, seems to be rising.
beats.means: Both point the same way: rates may need to go higher. Better-than-expected growth in China, Australia's biggest customer, also helps.
beats.fx: Hike talk → higher Australian rates ahead → support for the Aussie. A firmer US dollar on Fed hike bets is the brake.

impact.why: Officials' hawkish comments keep a November hike alive.

items.watch: Australia's July-September inflation figures, due late October, the last big input before the November 3 decision.

items.headline: UK inflation jumps more than expected fuelling rate hike expectations
items.story_title: UK: inflation, borrowing and the Oct 28 budget
items.summary: Alongside hotter inflation, UK government borrowing for September came in above forecast, a week before Chancellor Rachel Reeves' budget on October 28.

beats.was: UK government bond yields hit a 19-year high in September on worries about how much the government borrows, and the budget lands October 28.
beats.happened: The government borrowed £24.5bn in September, more than expected. Borrowing so far this tax year is about £6bn above the official forecast, and total debt passed £3 trillion for the first time.
beats.means: Higher borrowing leaves less room in the budget and keeps debt worries alive, at the same time as inflation pushes the Bank of England toward a hike.
beats.fx: Rate hikes help the pound, but debt worries hurt it. Together they cancelled out on Wednesday morning: the pound barely moved.

impact.why: Debt worries offset the lift from a likely rate hike.

items.watch: The October 28 budget: tax rises or spending cuts that calm bond markets would help the pound.

items.headline: Japanese Yen ticks up within previous range, buoyed by hawkish BoJ comments
items.story_title: BoJ: the road to the next hike
items.summary: Bank of Japan Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino said Japan's underlying inflation is close to the 2% goal, leaving room for more rate hikes; the yen edged up but stayed near 158 per dollar.

beats.was: The yen has been weak for weeks, near 158 per dollar, partly because Japan's rates are far below US rates. Markets expect the Bank of Japan to raise rates again, most likely on December 17.
beats.happened: Himino said underlying inflation is near target, borrowing conditions are still easy, and longer-run inflation expectations are rising.
beats.means: A deputy governor saying inflation is near target is a hint that the bank is getting ready to raise rates again.
beats.fx: More signals of a hike → smaller gap with US rates over time → slow support for the yen. A wider-than-expected trade deficit in September limited the lift.

impact.why: Supports the case for a December Bank of Japan hike, which is already expected.

items.watch: The Bank of Japan meeting next week, and whether it raises its inflation forecasts.

items.headline: US Dollar Index (DXY) Near Three-Week Low as Euro and Yen Firm
items.story_title: Fed: hold now, hike in December?
items.summary: The US dollar index sits near a three-week low around 101.6 as bets on a Federal Reserve hike at next week's meeting faded, with the move pushed to December instead.

beats.was: Hot US inflation figures on October 14 lifted the dollar index to about 102.9 on talk of a Fed hike as soon as October 28.
beats.happened: Markets now price about an 83% chance the Fed holds next week and about 94% for a hike in December. A firmer euro and yen did the rest.
beats.means: The Fed is still seen raising rates, just later. That takes some shine off the dollar now without changing the bigger picture.
beats.fx: Hike pushed back → less near-term pull for the dollar → it drifts lower against the euro and yen. A hawkish message next week could bring it back.

impact.why: A later Fed hike removes some near-term support.

items.watch: The Fed decision on October 28 and what Chair Kevin Warsh says about December.

items.headline: New Zealand Dollar softens below 0.5700 on RBNZ rate hike odds, CPI inflation data in focus
items.story_title: RBNZ: the October 28 decision
items.summary: The New Zealand dollar slipped to about 56.8 US cents, ending four days of gains, ahead of New Zealand's July-September inflation figures.

beats.was: Markets price about an 80% chance that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raises its rate by a quarter point to 3.00% on October 28.
beats.happened: Economists expect inflation to ease to 3.8% over the year from 4.1%, still above the bank's 1-3% target band. RBNZ chief economist Paul Conway said rates are most likely heading up but called the October decision wide open.
beats.means: This is the last inflation reading before the decision, so it can firm up or shake the hike bets.
beats.fx: Hotter than 3.8% → hike locked in → support for the kiwi; softer → hike in doubt → kiwi gives back its recent gains.

impact.why: A preview: the kiwi's direction depends on the inflation figure.

items.watch: New Zealand's quarterly inflation release, due within the next day.

items.headline: United Kingdom CPI inflation climbs to 3.5% YoY in September, vs. 3.4% expected
items.story_title: BoE: the November decision
items.summary: UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September, a touch above the 3.4% forecast and the highest in a year, as fuel costs from the US-Iran war fed into prices.

beats.was: The Bank of England, whose rate is 3.75% against a 2% inflation target, has not raised rates since 2023, but a strong jobs report had markets nearly sure of a quarter-point hike at its November 5 meeting.
beats.happened: Prices rose 3.5% over the year to September, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% expected. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, about as forecast.
beats.means: Inflation is running well above the 2% goal and moving the wrong way, mostly from petrol and diesel. That makes a November hike very hard for the Bank to skip.
beats.fx: Higher inflation → November hike all but locked in → UK rates stay attractive → support for the pound. Most of this was already expected, so the lift is modest.

impact.why: A higher-than-expected figure backs a November Bank of England hike.

items.watch: Whether the Bank signals more than one hike; a quick fall in oil would ease the pressure.

items.headline: US intel says Putin ordered NATO sabotage drive, Leipzig drone attack an opening shot
items.story_title: Russia–NATO: sabotage and grey-zone attacks
items.summary: The Wall Street Journal reports US intelligence concluded Russian President Vladimir Putin personally ordered a sabotage campaign against NATO countries, including an August drone attack on a German airport.

beats.was: Since August Europe has seen a string of suspected Russian attacks short of war: arson in Estonia and Poland, damage to Starlink stations and drone hits on ships in the Black Sea. Germany blamed Russia in September for a failed drone strike on a military-aid plane at Leipzig-Halle airport.
beats.happened: Citing European officials, the Journal says US intelligence found the campaign was ordered by Putin and run by a Russian military-intelligence unit. Aides to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said heavy casualties at Leipzig would have led Germany to weigh NATO's mutual-defence clause. Russia denies any role.
beats.means: It puts a name on attacks already known rather than reporting a new one, but it raises the chance of a tougher European response.
beats.fx: More security risk on Europe's doorstep → small weight on the euro and a small pull toward the franc as shelter. Little effect unless governments act. The lens: any new sanctions or a hit to Russian fuel supply?

impact.why: Raises the risk of a sharper Russia–NATO standoff near the euro area.
Mild extra demand for a safe place to park money.

items.watch: A formal European response or new sanctions; any disruption to Russian diesel exports.

items.headline: PBOC sets USD/CNY mid-point today at 6.7192 (vs. estimate at 6.6779)
items.story_title: China: Beijing slows the yuan's climb
items.summary: China's central bank set the yuan's daily reference rate about 0.6% weaker than analysts expected, another sign Beijing wants to slow the currency's rise.

beats.was: Each morning the People's Bank of China sets a midpoint for the yuan, which can trade 2% either side of it. Since late last year it has often set it weaker than models predict, to slow a yuan that has been near its strongest in over three years.
beats.happened: The bank set the rate at 6.7192 per dollar, against a Reuters estimate of 6.6779, a gap of about 0.6%. It gave no reason, which is normal.
beats.means: Beijing is still leaning against a fast-rising yuan, likely to protect exporters. It is a familiar move, not a new policy.
beats.fx: A softer yuan on purpose → China's trade partners get a little less lift from it → slight weight on the Aussie and kiwi, which trade as China proxies. The lens: does the gap keep widening?

impact.why: A held-back yuan takes a little shine off China-linked currencies.
Same China link, smaller effect.

items.watch: Whether the daily gap to estimates grows larger; China's next round of growth support.

items.headline: Euro weakens below 1.1250 as French protests and fiscal risks weigh
items.story_title: France: unrest, budget vote and the euro
items.summary: The euro slipped to about $1.1225 as France prepared to use some military forces to keep order during new protests expected this weekend.

beats.was: France has seen widespread protests over its budget, and investors already ask about 1.5 percentage points more to lend to France for ten years than to Germany, a sign of worry about its debts.
beats.happened: Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said curfews would be used where needed, and officials plan to bring in some troops for this weekend's protests. The euro fell back below $1.125 in Asian trading. ECB President Christine Lagarde and other ECB officials speak later Wednesday.
beats.means: Unrest in the eurozone's second-largest economy keeps a lid on the euro even when oil eases.
beats.fx: More unrest in France → more worry about French debt → investors demand more to hold it → weaker euro. The lens: calm protests and a passed budget would ease this.

impact.why: French unrest and debt worries weigh on the single currency.
Europe's worries send some money to the franc next door.

items.watch: This weekend's French protests, ECB speeches Wednesday, and France's budget vote on October 27.

items.headline: Japan's Katayama sees no gap with BOJ, says wage-driven inflation is near
items.story_title: BoJ: when the next hike comes
items.summary: Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told parliament the government and the Bank of Japan see things the same way, and that pay-driven inflation is close, a condition the BoJ wants before raising rates again.

beats.was: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government plans a consumption tax cut and cash handouts, and investors have worried it could clash with the Bank of Japan's rate rises; in September two board members picked by the government voted against the hike to 1.25%.
beats.happened: Katayama said today's price rises come mostly from import costs, but the economy is close to inflation driven by rising wages. Asked about a clash with the BoJ, she said the two sides talk and she sees no gap. She did not openly back more hikes.
beats.means: It lowers the odds that the government stands in the way of the next hike, which most economists expect in December.
beats.fx: Less political pushback → a December BoJ hike looks safer → mild support for the yen. The lens: do the government's picks on the board keep dissenting?

impact.why: Eases fears that the government blocks further rate rises.

items.watch: Friday's Japan inflation figures and the BoJ's Oct 29–30 meeting, including how its board votes.

items.headline: Oil rises on Middle East supply and shipping concerns
items.story_title: Hormuz: mines, tanker hits and blockade threats
items.summary: Brent crude climbed back toward $110 in Asian trading after Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a supertanker caught fire on a mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, and analysts said ship attacks now reach the Gulf of Oman.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, has been shut since the US-Iran war began this month, and Gulf exporters have leaned on loading points outside it, such as the Gulf of Oman, to keep crude moving.
beats.happened: Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said a supertanker hit a sea mine and caught fire south of the strait. LSEG analysts said attacks have spread as far as the Gulf of Oman; the ship tracker Kpler counts at least 18 attacks on vessels in two weeks. Yemen's Houthi rebels also claimed strikes on Saudi oil sites at Yanbu and Shaybah. Brent rose about 0.8% to $109.64.
beats.means: The workaround routes that kept Middle East oil flowing are now in range too, so a quick return to normal supply looks less likely even while mediation talks go on.
beats.fx: Attacks outside the strait → less oil getting out → higher crude → support for oil exporters like Canada, and a bigger import bill for Japan and Europe. The lens: do loadings in the Gulf of Oman actually slow?

impact.why: Attacks are reaching the routes used to bypass the shut strait.
Higher crude lifts Canada's export income.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a costlier barrel weighs on the yen.

items.watch: Whether tanker loadings off Oman drop, and any reply to Iran's mediation offer; Wednesday's US crude stock report.

items.headline: Japan exports rise 16.7% for 13th straight month on AI chip demand, trade gap narrows
items.story_title: Japan: exports, the oil bill and the yen
items.summary: Japan's exports grew 16.7% from a year earlier in September, a 13th straight rise but well short of the 20% expected, so the trade deficit came in wider than forecast at about ¥537 billion.

beats.was: Japan's exports have been lifted all year by demand for chips and AI equipment, while costly oil, pushed up by the Gulf war, has swollen the import bill and kept the country in trade deficit.
beats.happened: Japan's Ministry of Finance said September exports rose 16.7% from a year earlier, against about 20% expected and 19.3% in August. Imports rose 18.9%, slower than August's 28%. The deficit was about ¥537 billion, against ¥181 billion expected but half of August's roughly ¥1.1 trillion.
beats.means: Overseas demand for Japanese goods is still solid but cooling, and the energy bill remains the drag. A smaller gap than August helps a little, but the miss gives the Bank of Japan, which meets Oct 29–30, no new reason to hurry a rate rise.
beats.fx: Exports slower than hoped, oil still costly → more yen sold to pay for imports than expected → mild pressure on the yen. The lens: is the oil bill shrinking, or just pausing?

impact.why: Exports missed and the deficit beat forecasts, though it halved from August.

items.watch: The Bank of Japan's Oct 29–30 meeting and its new forecasts; a lasting drop in oil would shrink the import bill.

items.headline: Australian central banker says policy working, but inflation outlook worse
items.story_title: RBA: the November 3 decision
items.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia's deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, said inflation now looks set to run above the bank's own forecast, raising the odds of another rate rise on November 3. The Aussie pushed above 70 US cents.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia has already raised its cash rate four times this year, to 4.60%, to fight inflation lifted partly by the Gulf war's hit to oil. It next decides on November 3.
beats.happened: Speaking at a Citi conference in Sydney, Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said higher rates are slowing the economy, but the inflation outlook has got clearly worse, partly because of high oil prices. Markets raised the chance of a November hike to 4.85% to about 40%, from 30% at the start of the week, and AUD/USD rose to about 0.701, a two-week high.
beats.means: A senior official saying inflation will beat the bank's forecast keeps a fifth hike on the table, even with unemployment at a five-year high of 4.7% and house prices falling. Next week's third-quarter inflation figure, seen near 4%, is the deciding number.
beats.fx: Inflation running hotter than the RBA expected → more chance of a rate rise → higher returns on Australian dollars → Aussie up. The lens: does next week's inflation figure back him up?

impact.why: Hike odds for Nov 3 rose to about 40% and the Aussie broke above 0.70.

items.watch: Australia's third-quarter inflation figure next week; a soft print, or weaker jobs and housing, would cool hike bets.

items.headline: BOJ seen lifting rates to 1.50% in December as 69% of economists expect a Q4 hike
items.story_title: BoJ: when the next hike comes
items.summary: A Reuters poll of 78 economists found 69% now expect the Bank of Japan to raise rates to 1.50% by year-end, almost double September's share, with December the favourite month.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan raised its rate in June and again in September, to 1.25%, but the yen has stayed close to its weakest level of the year because US rates are far higher.
beats.happened: In the poll, taken Oct 13–19, 54 of 78 economists expect a hike to 1.50% this quarter, up from 36% a month ago. About 80% of those naming a month picked December; only 2% expect a move at the meeting ending Oct 30. Half now see rates reaching 2% or more.
beats.means: Forecasters see the BoJ moving faster than they thought a month ago, but not next week.
beats.fx: More hikes expected → Japan's rate gap with the US narrows over time → slow support for the yen. The lens: does the BoJ hint at December when it meets Oct 30?

impact.why: Economists now expect a quicker climb in Japan's rates.

items.watch: The BoJ's Oct 29–30 statement and new forecasts; most in the poll warned that more board dissent could weigh on the yen.

items.headline: Milk powder gains fuel GDT price surge
items.story_title: NZ dairy prices
items.summary: World dairy prices rose 2.5% at Tuesday's Global Dairy Trade auction, the most since February, led by the milk powders New Zealand sells most.

beats.was: The Global Dairy Trade auction runs twice a month and sets prices for New Zealand's biggest export, so it feeds farm incomes and the kiwi.
beats.happened: The overall index rose 2.5%. Whole milk powder gained 4.4% and skim milk powder 3.4%, while butter and milk fat slipped.
beats.means: Milk powder is what most decides NZ farmers' milk price, so forecasts for this season's payout may rise. Fonterra could update its forecast before its Nov 12 shareholder meeting.
beats.fx: Higher dairy prices → more export income for New Zealand → more demand for kiwi. The lens: does the gain hold at the next auction in early November?

impact.why: Best auction since February, led by the main export product.

items.watch: Fonterra's milk price forecast and NZ third-quarter inflation figures this week.

items.headline: BoE's Greene warns stalled wage disinflation raises inflation risks
items.story_title: BoE: the November decision
items.summary: Bank of England rate-setter Megan Greene said UK pay growth has stopped cooling at a level too high for 2% inflation, and the Bank should act early against it.

beats.was: Megan Greene sits on the Bank of England's nine-member rate committee and has long been one of its firmest voices for keeping rates high.
beats.happened: In a speech a day before UK inflation figures, she said pay growth has stalled above what fits a 2% inflation target and the risk of higher prices feeding into wages is bigger than the Bank thought.
beats.means: It backs the case for a hike at the Nov 5 meeting, which markets already price almost fully. It's one known hawk repeating her view, so it adds weight rather than news.
beats.fx: Sticky pay → more pressure to hike → UK yields stay high → support for the pound. The lens: do other committee members say the same?

impact.why: A rate-setter backing early action; a Nov 5 hike was already near fully priced.

items.watch: Wednesday's UK consumer prices: a soft figure would weaken her case.

items.headline: Canadian Dollar climbs to one-month highs as Bank of Canada hike bets grow
items.story_title: BoC: the October 28 decision
items.summary: The Canadian dollar reached its strongest in a month, about 1.405 per US dollar, as traders lean toward a Bank of Canada rate rise on October 28.

beats.was: The Bank of Canada has not raised rates this year. Canada's inflation rose to 3.1% in September, just under the 3.2% forecast, and Alberta voters on Monday chose to stay in Canada.
beats.happened: Canadian bond yields rose as more traders expect the bank's first hike of the year next week. A softer US dollar, lower US yields and oil near $110 added support.
beats.means: The loonie has a rate story, an oil story and less political risk all pulling the same way.
beats.fx: Expected Bank of Canada hike → higher Canadian yields → more demand for the loonie; dear oil adds export income. The lens: a sharp oil drop or a cautious bank would undo it.

impact.why: Hike bets, oil and less political risk all support the loonie.
A softer dollar and lower US yields helped the move.

items.watch: The Bank of Canada decision on October 28 and oil prices.

items.headline: British Pound surges to 1.3400 as UK jobs beat, Iran deal hopes grow
items.story_title: BoE: the November decision
items.summary: The pound gained about 0.7% to near 1.34 as a strong jobs report met a softer dollar on US-Iran hopes.

beats.was: Sterling's move after the UK jobs report and the US-Iran reports.
beats.happened: The UK added about 102,000 jobs in three months, well above forecasts, and unemployment fell. Markets now see about a 93% chance of a November BoE hike.
beats.means: Two forces lined up at once: a firmer case for UK rates and a weaker dollar. The pound sits right under a cluster of resistance near 1.341.
beats.fx: Strong jobs → BoE hike nearly certain → higher UK yields → pound up; softer dollar adds to it. The lens: does CPI confirm?

impact.why: Up about 0.7% to five-week highs, building on the jobs beat.
Softer on US-Iran hopes and weak housing data.

items.watch: Wednesday's UK CPI; a denial of the US-Iran plan would help the dollar back.

items.headline: Euro climbs as Oil prices tumble on US-Iran negotiation hopes
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: The dollar index slipped to its lowest since Oct 1 as oil and US 10-year yields fell on US-Iran talks hope. EUR/USD rose to about 1.125.

beats.was: The euro-dollar rate during the US session.
beats.happened: EUR/USD rose about 0.35% to near 1.125. The dollar index fell to about 101.55, off last week's 18-month high near 103, and the US 10-year yield dropped about 6 basis points to around 5.08%.
beats.means: The dollar's recent strength rode on oil-driven yields. When oil eases, that support fades, and Europe, a big oil importer, gets some relief.
beats.fx: Oil down → US yields down → dollar's yield edge narrows → dollar slips, euro gains. The lens: does oil keep falling?

impact.why: Dollar index fell to a near three-week low as yields dropped.
Cheaper oil eases Europe's import bill and lifts the euro.

items.watch: Houthi strikes and Hormuz ship attacks are still live; a fresh hit would send oil and the dollar back up.

items.headline: Canadian Dollar: market pricing seen excessive despite hike bets (BBH)
items.story_title: BoC: the October 28 decision
items.summary: A strategist at the bank Brown Brothers Harriman argues markets expect too many Bank of Canada rate rises, which limits how far the Canadian dollar can climb.

beats.was: Traders have quickly raised their bets on a Bank of Canada rate hike on October 28, to about 78% in swaps from 60%, after Governor Tiff Macklem warned that inflation risks are spreading.
beats.happened: Elias Haddad of Brown Brothers Harriman noted that September's headline inflation of 3.1% came mostly from energy, while the bank's preferred core measures eased to about 1.85%, below its 2% target. He judged the roughly one percentage point of hikes priced over the next year as too much.
beats.means: The case for a hike rests on oil-driven prices, not broad inflation, and the economy still has slack. If the bank sounds less eager than markets expect, the loonie's rate support could shrink.
beats.fx: Core inflation under target + spare capacity in the economy → fewer hikes than priced → caps the loonie's gains. The lens: a hawkish decision on October 28 would prove this wrong.

impact.why: Hike bets support the loonie, but soft core inflation argues markets have gone too far.

items.watch: The Bank of Canada decision and statement on October 28.

items.headline: Swiss Franc Recovery Tests SNB Tolerance Against Euro
items.story_title: Franc: haven demand vs the SNB
items.summary: The franc climbed to a three-month high against the euro on fears of a European debt crisis, nearing levels where the SNB has threatened to step in.

beats.was: The franc's comeback against the euro after months of weakness.
beats.happened: EUR/CHF fell to a three-month low as money sought shelter from Europe's debt worries and Switzerland's sounder public finances.
beats.means: The franc is near the zone where the SNB warned it could sell francs. That threat caps gains unless the euro area's problems get worse.
beats.fx: European debt fears → money into a safe, low-debt neighbour → franc up, until the SNB pushes back. The lens: does France's budget fight get worse?

impact.why: Haven demand lifted it, but the SNB's line is close.
Debt worries pushed it to a three-month low on the franc.

items.watch: Any SNB intervention or warning; France's Oct 27 budget vote.

items.headline: Yen jumps after JGB auction draws big demand, euro finds relief
items.story_title: Japan: tax cuts and the bond bill
items.summary: Buyers swamped Japan's 20-year bond sale with record demand, pulling yields down and giving the yen its first gain in three days.

beats.was: Japan sold 20-year government bonds, a test of whether investors will fund its growing borrowing.
beats.happened: Bids came in at 5.84 times the amount on offer, the most since these bonds began in 1987, against 4.01 last month. The 20-year yield fell 6bp to 3.71% and the yen rose to about 158.1 per dollar.
beats.means: Fears that Japan's tax cuts would scare off bond buyers eased for now, and some investors see Japanese bonds as a calmer place than France. It eases one source of yen weakness, but the gap with US rates is still wide.
beats.fx: Strong bond demand → less fear over Japan's debt → steadier yields and money staying home → yen firmer. The lens: is Japan's fiscal risk fading or just paused?

impact.why: Record auction demand eased debt fears and snapped a two-day slide.
Edged up to about 1.123 as pressure from France eased overnight.

items.watch: Friday's Japan CPI and any sign the auction demand doesn't repeat; a US yield jump would undo the gain.

items.headline: US pending home sales tumble to record low in September
items.story_title: US housing: frozen by 7%+ mortgages
items.summary: Signed home-sale contracts fell 7.3% in September to the lowest level on record, far worse than the small dip expected. Mortgage rates above 7% are freezing buyers.

beats.was: Pending home sales count contracts signed on existing homes, an early read on sales a month or two ahead.
beats.happened: Contracts fell 7.3% in a month, against a 0.5% dip forecast, and are down about 11% on a year ago. Every region fell.
beats.means: War-driven inflation pushed Treasury yields up, and 30-year mortgages near 7.4% have priced many buyers out. Housing is where high rates bite first, so the US economy is starting to feel the squeeze.
beats.fx: Housing slumps → growth cools → less room for the Fed to keep hiking → softer yield support → dollar loses a little shine. The lens: does the weakness spread past housing?

impact.why: A record-low print, far below forecast, shows high rates starting to hurt growth.

items.watch: If mortgage rates ease or other data hold firm, this stays a housing story rather than a growth scare.

items.headline: Middle East War: Attempted strikes on US ships 'unsuccessful', Hegseth visits region
items.story_title: Saudi–Houthi fighting and the Gulf supply risk
items.summary: US crude jumped about 6% toward $110 as the Houthis fired at Riyadh again and the US defence chief made a surprise trip to the region. Iran's attempts to hit US ships near Hormuz reportedly failed.

beats.was: A day of war news around the Gulf: Houthi missiles at Saudi Arabia, Iran's mines in Hormuz, and a surprise visit by the US defence secretary.
beats.happened: A Houthi missile aimed at Riyadh was intercepted and the city's airport stayed shut. US crude rose about 5.7% to roughly $109.60 and Brent about 2% to near $111.70.
beats.means: Oil is pricing more than one route at risk at once: Hormuz and the Saudi coast. A senior US visit suggests next steps are being weighed, so traders keep paying for the risk.
beats.fx: More attacks → more fear for supply → dearer oil → oil sellers like the loonie gain, oil buyers like Japan pay more → yen under pressure. The lens: does any oil actually stop flowing?

impact.why: US crude up about 6% in a day as attacks spread to more targets.
Canada sells oil, so a higher price helps its trade.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a dearer barrel drains it.
War headlines keep some shelter demand under the franc.

items.watch: Any confirmed halt in Saudi or Hormuz exports would push this higher; a US–Iran deal or a lull in attacks would pull it back.

items.headline: Oil prices hit five-month high as Houthi escalation worsens supply and inflation fears
items.story_title: Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia
items.summary: Brent climbed past $111, its highest since May, after a string of Houthi attacks on Saudi targets and with Gulf shipping still squeezed.

beats.was: The price of oil, which sets fuel and import bills for every economy and the export income of producers like Canada.
beats.happened: Brent rose about 1.5% to near $111 and US crude to about $101, five-month highs, after the Houthis claimed six attacks on Saudi Arabia on Monday. Emergency stock releases and letting sanctioned tankers sail again have not offset the hit.
beats.means: Supply from the Gulf is still tight and each new attack adds to the risk premium. Dearer fuel feeds inflation, which keeps central banks, the Fed included, leaning toward higher rates.
beats.fx: Oil up → more income for exporters, bigger bills for importers → loonie supported, yen and euro squeezed, and more inflation pressure keeping US yields high. The lens: is Gulf supply getting through or not?

impact.why: Five-month high as attacks keep Gulf supply tight.
Higher crude lifts Canada's export income.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so dearer crude drains the yen.
Oil-driven inflation keeps rate-hike bets and yields up, a drag on gold.

items.watch: A US-Iran deal or proof that Hormuz traffic is recovering would pull the premium out; a confirmed hit to Saudi output would add to it.

items.headline: Sterling rises as strong labour market data reinforces rate hike bets
items.story_title: BoE: the November decision
items.summary: UK jobs held up better than feared: unemployment slipped to 4.7% and pay beat forecasts, so a November BoE hike now looks close to a done deal.

beats.was: The UK's monthly jobs report: how many people are out of work and how fast pay is rising.
beats.happened: Unemployment fell to 4.7%, its lowest since mid-2025, and regular pay grew 3.7% a year, faster than expected. Payrolls edged up and vacancies slipped under 700,000.
beats.means: A labour market this firm keeps wage-driven inflation alive, which removes the BoE's main excuse to wait. Markets now price a November 5 hike almost fully.
beats.fx: Firm jobs and pay → BoE more likely to hike → higher UK yields → money into sterling → pound up. The lens: does Wednesday's CPI back it up?

impact.why: Jobs and pay beat, locking in a November hike; up about 0.3% on the dollar and the euro.
Lost ground to sterling, which sits near its best level on the euro since May 2025.

items.watch: Wednesday's UK CPI: a soft print would cool the hike talk; a hot one would add to it.

items.headline: Canadian Dollar Outperforms on Alberta Vote
items.story_title: Alberta votes to stay in Canada
items.summary: About three in four Alberta voters rejected starting a path to separation, lifting a political risk off the loonie. It gained on the dollar and the euro.

beats.was: A nonbinding Alberta referendum on whether to start a legal process toward leaving Canada. Alberta is the country's main oil province.
beats.happened: Unofficial results show about 76% voted to stay, a clear margin. USD/CAD slid to about 1.4056, down roughly 1.6% from last week's high.
beats.means: A split would have put Canada's oil income in doubt. A decisive no removes that discount and leaves the loonie trading on oil and the Bank of Canada again.
beats.fx: Separation risk off the table → less reason to hold back from Canadian assets → loonie up. The lens: with politics settled, how hawkish is the BoC on Oct 28?

impact.why: A decisive vote to stay removed a risk premium; up about 0.4% on the dollar and euro.

items.watch: The official tally on Oct 29; a much narrower count would revive the doubt.
